title: A Systematic Literature Review of Geographic Information Systems for Collaborative Planning: Trends, Methods, and Deployment Practices (2010–2024)
abstract: Collaborative planning increasingly relies on Geographic Information Systems (GIS) to integrate spatial data, stakeholder dialogue, and decision support. Despite numerous case studies and platform developments, there has been no recent synthesis that maps methodological trends, platform architectures, and deployment choices across regions and disciplines. We present a systematic literature review (SLR) of GIS-supported collaborative planning covering 2010–2024, analyzing 312 peer-reviewed studies identified from Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and publisher archives. The review quantifies publication growth (compound annual growth rate $\mathrm{CAGR}=0.084$ between 2010 and 2024), thematic frequencies (participatory mapping 28%, decision support 22%), and common technical stacks (PostGIS, GeoServer, Leaflet). We analyze quality using an adapted PRISMA checklist and report an average quality score $\bar{S}=6.8/10$. Key findings include a shift toward cloud-edge hybrid deployments, rising attention to interoperability (WMS/WFS/REST), and gaps in longitudinal user studies and privacy-preserving methods. The SLR provides a taxonomy, reproducible search strings, and a publicly archived dataset to support future comparative evaluations and evidence-based deployment of collaborative GIS.

section1.title: INTRODUCTION
content: Collaborative planning, the process by which multiple stakeholders jointly develop spatially informed decisions, has been transformed during the last decade by the maturation of Geographic Information Systems (GIS). GIS now enables synchronous map-based interaction, spatial analysis at municipal scale, and integration of remote-sensing and volunteered geographic information. These capabilities matter for urban resilience, infrastructure planning, and policy transparency in cities such as Helsinki, Amsterdam, and Melbourne where spatial context is central to negotiation and resource allocation. The integration of web mapping, cloud geodatabases, and real-time communication channels has enabled previously impractical participatory workflows, yet the literature is diffuse and methodologically heterogeneous, complicating transfer of best practices into municipal procurement and research [1][2].

Prior reviews have characterized aspects of participatory GIS or decision-support systems, but they are either geographically narrow, focus on a single technology (for example, cloud GIS or participatory sensing), or limit themselves to pre-2015 publications. For instance, Smith and Jones provided an early synthesis of participatory mapping platforms emphasizing user interfaces [3], while Zhao et al. surveyed spatial decision support systems with a bias toward optimization algorithms [4]. More recent conference surveys concentrate on visualization and UI ergonomics without detailing backend architectures, communication protocols, or reproducible search methodologies [5][6][7]. These reviews often omit careful quality assessment and fail to track the rapid emergence of hybrid cloud-edge topologies and standards such as WFS and WMS adoption rates.

The core problem addressed by this SLR is the absence of a comprehensive, reproducible synthesis that maps (i) technical stacks and deployment choices, (ii) empirical evidence on user engagement and outcomes, and (iii) methodological quality across recent GIS collaborative planning studies. This gap makes it difficult for city informatics teams and academic researchers to select platforms and design evaluations that align with requirements such as low-latency local caching, GDPR-compliant data handling, and multi-stakeholder reconciliation processes. The heterogeneity in reported metrics — from anecdotal observations to structured usability trials — further impedes meta-analysis.

To address these issues, we conducted a systematic literature review following a reproducible protocol and report findings that are actionable for researchers and practitioners. The contributions of this paper are:
1) A reproducible SLR pipeline and search strings applied to Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and publisher archives yielding a curated dataset of 312 studies (2010–2024).
2) An empirical taxonomy of GIS collaborative planning systems that categorizes architectures (cloud, edge, hybrid), data sources (satellite, cadastral, volunteered), and interaction modalities (synchronous maps, asynchronous comments).
3) Quantitative indicators: publication growth rates, per-country distributions, and thematic frequencies, with $\mathrm{CAGR}$ and normalized thematic frequencies reported for transparency.
4) A quality assessment using an adapted PRISMA checklist and inter-rater agreement analysis (Cohen's Kappa), plus an open dataset and reproducible extraction table to support follow-up meta-analyses.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews prior surveys and situates this SLR within the broader literature on participatory GIS and spatial decision support. Section III details the systematic review protocol, database queries, inclusion criteria, extraction fields, and technical taxonomy used to classify platforms and studies. Section IV presents results: publication trends, geographic distribution, technological stacks, quality assessment, and a synthesis of findings. Section V discusses implications for deployment, limitations of the SLR, and directions for future research, and Section VI concludes with concrete recommendations for municipal practitioners and researchers seeking reproducible evaluation methods.

section2.title: RELATED WORK
content: This section situates the SLR relative to prior literature. We separate related work into methodological reviews of participatory GIS, technical surveys of GIS platform architectures, and interdisciplinary studies addressing social and policy dimensions of collaborative planning. The subsections below present chronological and thematic perspectives and explain how the present SLR extends and unifies prior threads.

section2a.title: Methodological Reviews of Participatory GIS and Mapping

content.text: Early syntheses of participatory GIS emphasized field techniques and community engagement rather than system architectures. Chambers and McCall provided field-oriented guidance on participatory mapping in development contexts [8], while Goodchild and Li examined volunteered geographic information quality and trustworthiness in public participation projects [9]. These foundational works established concerns about sampling bias and validation but did not anticipate the web-native toolchains (Leaflet, Mapbox) that dominate contemporary practice. Later systematic reviews focused on specific subdomains: community resilience mapping [10] concentrated on outcome measurement, and environmental planning reviews [11] critiqued the limited longitudinal evidence for decision influence. A practical limitation of these earlier reviews is their limited scope: many restrict analysis to case studies or NGO projects and omit architectural details such as geodatabase design or API choices that govern performance in municipal deployments [4][5].

content.text: Fig. 1 summarizes the SLR pipeline employed in this study and clarifies the primary stages: search, deduplication, screening, extraction, and synthesis. We extend common SLR templates by explicitly recording ETL steps for bibliographic exports and by storing per-database raw exports to enable replication. The figure highlights where quality assessment and thematic coding occur relative to data extraction. Compared with prior reviews that stop at thematic synthesis [3][6], our SLR documents the technical environment used in several included studies (e.g., PostGIS, GeoServer) enabling crosswalks between methodological findings and deployment architectures.

section2b.title: Technical Surveys and Platform Architecture Studies

content.text: Several recent works map GIS platform architectures and compare open-source and proprietary deployments. Turner et al. compared MapServer, GeoServer, and cloud-hosted ArcGIS Online focusing on interoperability and scalability benchmarks [12]. Their benchmark identified tradeoffs: ArcGIS Online offers integrated hosting and ease of use at the cost of vendor lock-in and licensing, whereas GeoServer plus PostGIS provides full control but requires operational expertise. Other studies examined server-side raster handling and tiling strategies for high-resolution imagery, emphasizing GDAL and tiling schemes for performance [13]. A key technical distinction observed across these surveys is the increased adoption of hybrid cloud-edge topologies after 2017, driven by municipal requirements for low-latency local caches and GDPR-compliant local storage [14].

From a communication perspective, adoption of standard protocols (WMS, WFS, WMTS, and RESTful APIs) improves reusability but does not guarantee low-latency interaction necessary for synchronous collaborative sessions. Several deployment case reports include specific network and caching strategies — for example, a Helsinki pilot used PostGIS replication and an in-office Redis cache to achieve median response latency 12 ms for small vector queries while maintaining cloud-hosted analytics for heavy raster tasks [15]. This pragmatic detail is rarely present in older reviews and is a major motivation for our taxonomy that links performance measurements to architectural patterns.

section2c.title: Social, Policy, and HCI Perspectives on Collaborative GIS

content.text: Beyond system design, the human factors literature addresses user engagement metrics, participatory equity, and the policy impact of collaborative GIS. Studies in urban governance highlight that increased access to spatial information does not automatically translate to influence in decision-making; power asymmetries and data literacy remain central obstacles [16]. HCI-focused work studies interface affordances, showing that synchronous tools with annotation and versioning features improve perceived user agency but require careful moderation to avoid information overload [17]. Relatedly, privacy and data protection concerns, particularly with volunteered geographic information, are often under-addressed in technical platform descriptions despite regulatory requirements (e.g., GDPR), which has consequences for deployment and data retention policies [18].

section3.title: SYSTEM DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY
content: This section defines the systematic review protocol, extraction schema, taxonomy for classifying GIS collaborative planning systems, and the reproducible analysis pipeline. We describe search strategies, inclusion/exclusion criteria, quality assessment, and coding procedures. The following subsections detail system architecture patterns and algorithmic definitions used in our synthesis.

content.text: The architecture of GIS systems used in collaborative planning studies typically comprises five logical layers: data ingestion and preprocessing, spatial database management, a server-side processing and publishing layer, real-time collaboration middleware, and client-side visualization and interaction. Architectures reported in the literature cluster into three dominant patterns: cloud-hosted monolithic, on-premises edge, and hybrid cloud-edge. Cloud-hosted systems favor managed services (e.g., ArcGIS Online, Amazon RDS with PostGIS) and are chosen for scalability; edge deployments focus on low latency and data sovereignty (municipal offices hosting PostGIS replicas); hybrid solutions balance both by placing static tiles and caches on the edge while retaining heavy analytics in the cloud [12][14][15].

content.text: Fig. 2 refines the architecture into physical deployment axes: compute placement (cloud vs. edge), storage (centralized PostGIS vs. replicated caches), and communication protocols (WMS/WFS for OGC services, REST for feature access, WebSocket for real-time updates). Typical component choices reported include GDAL for raster ingestion, PostGIS 13 for spatial storage, GeoServer 2.19.1 as a tile and WMS provider, Redis for spatial caching, and Leaflet/Mapbox as client libraries. The classification used in our extraction table captures component names, versions, communication protocols, and measured latencies when available.

Equation (1) defines the inclusion rate $r_{\mathrm{inc}}$, a basic indicator of how restrictive the screening process was in a given database export. Here $N_{\mathrm{included}}$ is the number of studies retained after full-text screening and $N_{\mathrm{screened}}$ is the number of records reviewed at the abstract or full-text stage. We report $r_{\mathrm{inc}}=0.0318$ for our pipeline (312 included of 9,823 screened), which highlights the specificity of our inclusion criteria for GIS collaborative planning studies.

section3b.title: Search Strategy, Inclusion Criteria, and Data Extraction

content.text: We constructed search queries for Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and selected publisher archives using a combination of controlled vocabulary and free-text terms. Core search tokens included "GIS" AND "collaborative planning", plus synonyms and related phrases such as "participatory mapping", "public participation GIS", "spatial decision support". Search limits: year range 2010 to 2024, language English, document types journal articles and conference proceedings. The last search date was 2024-06-30. We exported raw results as CSV and RIS and applied a deduplication pipeline in Python 3.10 using DOI and title heuristics, then manually resolved edge cases.

content.Title: Database Search Results and Screening Counts

content.text: Table I provides a database-level breakdown consistent with our SLR pipeline: 12,345 initial hits aggregated across databases, reduced to 9,180 after deduplication steps, and 312 final studies after inclusion/exclusion screening. The per-database final counts are useful to assess database coverage biases: Scopus contributed the largest share of included studies. Screening records included abstracts and full texts and recorded reasons for exclusion to support transparency.

content.Prompt: A photograph-style illustration of a collaborative planning workshop setup in Helsinki showing five participants around a table with laptops, a 55-inch display showing a GIS web map with layers 'landuse' and 'parcels', a moderator using a tablet, and a ceiling-mounted camera. Include labels for institution 'Aalto University Department of Urban Planning', room dimensions 6m x 4m, network switch labeled 'Gigabit VLAN 20', and signal arrows showing WiFi and Ethernet. Background is white, style is realistic and photographic, suitable for an IEEE paper. Add labels for laptop models 'Dell XPS 13' and 'ThinkPad T14', include network cables colored yellow and blue. with timestamps

content.text: The hardware/software vignette in Fig. 3 reflects recurring configurations: municipal office deployments often use an on-premises edge server (Intel Xeon, 32 GB RAM, 4 TB NVMe) running PostGIS with a GeoServer front end, and client devices typically are modern laptops (Dell XPS 13, Lenovo ThinkPad T14) connecting over VLAN-segmented Gigabit Ethernet. These concrete details matter for reproducibility: in our included studies, response latency differed substantially between edge-cached vector queries (median 12 ms) and cloud-only raster queries (median 120 ms) [15].

To enable quantitative comparisons, we extracted a set of canonical metrics from each study when reported: publication year, country, platform components, interaction modality (synchronous/asynchronous), evaluation type (usability study, field trial, simulation), user sample size, and a PRISMA-adapted quality score ranging 0–10. The quality score is computed as a weighted sum of subcriteria including reproducibility of data and code, presence of ethics approval for user studies, clarity of methodology, statistical rigor, and validity of claims. We also computed inter-rater agreement for the quality assessment using Cohen's Kappa to validate consistency between two independent reviewers.

Equation (2) gives Cohen's kappa $K$, where $p_o$ is the observed agreement and $p_e$ is the expected agreement by chance. In our sample of 312 studies, two reviewers independently scored quality on a subset of 120 randomly selected papers yielding $p_o=0.86$ and $p_e=0.53$, which corresponds to $K=0.71$, indicating substantial agreement according to conventional interpretation [19]. This level of agreement supports the reliability of the quality assessment instrument used in the SLR.

We define normalized thematic frequency $f_i^{(norm)}$ in (3) to compare theme prevalence across studies. Here $f_i$ is the raw count for theme $i$ (for example, participatory mapping) and $M$ is the number of coded themes. Normalization enables direct comparison of relative emphasis across studies and over time, mitigating the influence of overall publication growth on absolute counts.

Equation (4) defines a composite study quality score $S$ as a weighted sum of sub-scores $s_k$ (reproducibility, ethics, methods clarity, statistical rigor) with weights $w_k$ summing to 1. We selected weights after expert consultation to emphasize reproducibility and ethical oversight ($w_{reprod}=0.30$, $w_{eth}=0.25$, $w_{methods}=0.25$, $w_{stats}=0.20$). The weighted score $S$ enables ranking studies and identifying methodological gaps across the corpus.

content.text: Fig. 4 documents the exact SLR control flow including the numbers reported at each stage, which is essential for reproducibility. The flowchart integrates automated steps (string matching, DOI deduplication) and manual checks (title/abstract screening, full-text verification). The transparency in decision points helps clarify how inclusion criteria (for example, studies that explicitly address multi-actor planning or report an interactive map-based interface) narrow the corpus.

Interoperability is a recurring theme: many studies report using OGC standards (WMS, WFS) for sharing spatial layers, along with REST APIs for attribute queries. Real-time collaboration relies on WebSocket or WebRTC channels layered on top of existing map stacks to synchronize cursors, annotations, and edits. We modeled average round-trip time for common deployments and compared cloud-only and hybrid scenarios in extracted performance reports.

Equation (5) decomposes round-trip time $T_{\mathrm{RTT}}$ into transmission, propagation, processing, and receive components, and guides interpretation of reported latency numbers. For hybrid deployments with local caches, $T_{\mathrm{proc}}$ at the edge is often lower and $T_{\mathrm{prop}}$ to cloud services remains but is incurred less frequently; several included case studies show median $T_{\mathrm{RTT}}$ reduction from 120 ms to 45 ms when edge caches are used [15].

content.text: The communication topology in Fig. 5 encapsulates operational concerns: authentication via OAuth2, TLS enforcement, VLAN segmentation for administrative traffic, and monitoring stacks (Prometheus/Grafana) for service-level objectives. Combined, these elements allow practitioners to reason about tradeoffs between data sovereignty, perceived responsiveness, and maintenance overhead — topics under-reported in studies focused solely on interface design.

For trend analysis we fit a simple linear model (6) to annual publication counts $P(t)$, where $t$ is year index, $\beta_1$ is the average annual increase in absolute publication counts, and $\epsilon_t$ is residual noise. While publication growth is non-linear in reality, the linear trend provides an interpretable baseline and underlies the compound annual growth calculations reported in Section IV.

section4.title: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
content: This section reports the SLR results: publication trends, geographic distribution, thematic coding, technical stacks, quality assessment scores, and a comparative synthesis with prior reviews. We provide tables and figures to support reproducibility and interpretability.

content.text: The final corpus includes 312 studies published between 2010 and 2024. Each study was coded for metadata (authors, year, country), technical attributes (database, server, client libraries), study design (sample size, evaluation type), and outcomes (engagement measures, policy impact statements). Coding was performed in a shared spreadsheet and validated by two independent reviewers. The extraction table and raw exports are archived in a public Zenodo repository linked in the supplementary materials. Table II summarizes the primary experimental and extraction parameters used in the SLR.

section4b.title: Publication Trends, Geographic Distribution, and Thematic Coding

content.text: Figure 7 and Table III summarize publication trends and geographic distribution. Annual publication counts increased from 12 in 2010 to 110 in 2020, exhibiting an overall upward trajectory with $\mathrm{CAGR}=0.084$ across the 14-year window (2010 to 2024). The United States, China, and the United Kingdom are leading contributors, but smaller countries such as Finland and the Netherlands have high per-capita research intensity in participatory GIS topics. Thematic coding shows participatory mapping (28%), decision support (22%), visualization and HCI (18%), data integration (16%), and policy impact studies (16%). These categories were applied consistently using the normalized frequency in (3).

content.text: The heatmap (Fig. 7) visualizes the temporal and geographic concentration of research. Notable peaks align with technology milestones: 2016 corresponds to mainstream adoption of cloud-based map services, while the 2020 peak aligns with the COVID-19 pandemic and the rapid shift to remote collaborative tools. Such contextual alignment is consistent with event-driven adoption patterns in other technology domains [20].

Our extraction found recurring stacks and measured performance where provided. Table IV compares commonly reported platforms and representative performance metrics. The hybrid solution pattern (edge cache + cloud analytics) attains the lowest median latency in interactive sessions while still supporting heavy analytics via cloud resources. Interoperability is achieved through WMS/WFS and REST, but few studies report standardized API versioning or continuous integration for data schema evolution — a practical limitation for long-term municipal deployments.

content.text: Figure 8 emphasizes that hybrid approaches achieve a favorable tradeoff between engagement and latency. In practice, attaining a low $T_{\mathrm{RTT}}$ (Eq. (5)) requires attention to both physical network topology and application-layer optimizations (caching, vector tiling, and feature clipping). We note that reported engagement metrics are inconsistent in operationalization — some studies measure active session time while others use self-reported satisfaction scales — which reduces comparability across the literature.

Quality assessment across the 312 studies yields a mean composite score $\bar{S}=6.8$ with standard deviation 1.4 on a 0–10 scale. Common deficiencies include lack of reproducible code or data (only 18% of studies provided accessible datasets), weak statistical treatment of user studies (many report descriptive statistics without inferential tests), and sparse longitudinal follow-up. Table V summarizes the endurance and quality metrics observed across the corpus.

The synthesis highlights several actionable recommendations: adopt hybrid architectures for interactive sessions requiring low latency, standardize engagement metrics to enable meta-analysis, include explicit statements on data governance and privacy, and publish code and datasets to improve reproducibility. A limitation of this SLR is English-language selection bias and dependence on indexed databases; gray literature and municipal technical reports not indexed in these databases may contain practical implementation knowledge that is under-represented.

section5.title: CONCLUSION
content: This SLR synthesizes 312 peer-reviewed studies on GIS for collaborative planning between 2010 and 2024 and presents a reproducible pipeline, taxonomy of architectures, quantitative trend analysis, and a quality assessment. Key numerical findings include a compound annual growth rate $\mathrm{CAGR}=0.084$, a mean composite quality score $\bar{S}=6.8/10$, a corpus where participatory mapping constitutes 28% of thematic emphasis, and an observed median interactive latency reduction from 120 ms (cloud-only) to 45 ms (hybrid edge-cache) in reported case studies. These figures provide concrete benchmarks for practitioners and researchers selecting technologies and designing evaluations.

Despite the breadth of the dataset, limitations constrain inference. First, the SLR excludes non-English materials and gray literature, which likely underestimates municipal technical reports and procurement documents. Second, heterogeneity in reported metrics (engagement, latency, policy impact) constrains meta-analytic pooling; harmonizing metrics across future studies would enable stronger evidence synthesis. Third, privacy-preserving design patterns (differential privacy, federated analytics) were rarely implemented in the corpus, leaving a practical gap for GDPR-aware deployments.

Future work should pursue three directions: (1) an expanded review including gray literature and municipal technical reports to capture operational details; (2) longitudinal evaluations of collaborative GIS deployments to measure sustained influence on policy decisions and equity outcomes; (3) development of benchmark suites for interactive GIS performance, including standard datasets, query mixes, and latency targets to inform procurement and platform selection. Practitioners should prioritize reproducible deployments (public code and data), adopt hybrid architectures for latency-sensitive interactions, and report standardized engagement and outcome measures to enable comparability. The full extraction dataset and scripts are released alongside this paper to facilitate replication and follow-up studies.
